Tides are the ocean’s slow, planetary breath, a rhythm set not by the sea itself but by the distant pull of the moon and, to a lesser extent, the sun. Imagine the Earth and its moon locked in a cosmic dance, each one’s gravity reaching out to the other. The moon’s pull is strongest on the side of our planet that faces it, drawing the water there into a slight, swelling bulge. On the opposite side of the Earth, a second, fainter bulge forms, not because the moon pulls that water away, but because it pulls the solid Earth itself more strongly than it pulls the water on the far side, leaving that water behind, as it were, in a counter-balancing heap. These two bulges are the high tides, and as the Earth spins on its axis once every twenty-four hours, any given coastline passes through both of them, experiencing two high tides and two low tides each day.

The sun adds its own, gentler hand to this choreography. When the sun, the moon, and the Earth line up—at the new and full moon—their gravitational forces combine, producing especially pronounced spring tides, where the water rises higher and falls lower than usual. When the sun and moon sit at right angles to each other, their pulls partially cancel out, creating the milder neap tides. The shape of the coastline, the depth of the sea floor, and the funneling of bays and estuaries all sculpt these fundamental bulges into the specific, local patterns we see, from the dramatic bore of a river mouth to the gentle lapping of a sheltered cove. So the next time you watch the water creep up the sand, you are witnessing the quiet, ceaseless conversation between our world and its nearest celestial companions, a gravitational tug-of-war played out in liquid time.
